open-question.question: When the completion procedure's discretionary read of past work fails — its `tasks <path> --with-body` call or its `show <milestone path>` follow-up exits non-zero, as `show` does on the `-` a task line prints for a commit joining no single milestone — what does the runner do: stop the task on a fixed line with the tool's `Error:` line beneath it, as the review pass and the starting-state procedure stop on a failed read of theirs, or carry on with the task without the read, as `ask-in-milestone-context` carries on after telling the failure in prose?
open-question.alternative: Any non-zero exit of the read's `tasks <path> --with-body` call or its `show <milestone path>` follow-up, at step 2 or step 3, whatever its `Error:` line says, is one unclassified condition: the procedure stops at once with no corrected retry, reporting a new fixed line of its own (a new row in the `## Fixed console lines` table of `docs/skill-reference.md`) first and the tool's `Error:` line verbatim beneath it. The inline `complete-task` skill prints that report; the `complete-task` agent returns `FAILED:` with the line as its reason, writing neither scratch file. A `-` path field reaching `show` is a failure like any other. The tree is left as it stands, untouched when the stop comes at step 2 and resumable when it comes at step 3. Matches the review pass and the starting-state procedure exactly, so every discretionary milestones-tool read that can fail has one rule across the plugin, and a harness sees from the fixed line which check ended the run rather than a task completed on a read that silently never happened. A read the procedure itself calls discretionary becomes able to end a whole unattended `complete-all-tasks` run (the agent's `FAILED:` stops the loop on `Task run stopped — a task failed.`), and it does so predictably on a valid input, since `show` refuses the `-` a task line prints for a commit joining no single milestone; it also adds a fixed line, a table row, and its rendering in every host tree.

The procedure says the `show` follow-up is taken only on a task line whose milestone field names a path, never on a `-` line, so the predictable refusal never occurs; every remaining failure of either call (git unavailable, a shallow or broken repository, a mistyped path `tasks` finds in neither tree nor history) stops the task as in a uniform stop: a new fixed line first, the `Error:` line beneath it, `FAILED:` with that line from the agent, nothing reverted. Keeps the plugin's stop-on-failed-read rule while removing the one failure that comes from a well-formed print rather than from a broken environment, so a stop always means something is actually wrong and a project with legacy or anomalous task commits does not stop every task that touches their files. Adds a clause about the `-` placeholder to the procedure (a tool detail the runtime prose otherwise leaves to the tool's help text) beside a new fixed line and table row, and still lets a discretionary read, on a git-level failure, end an unattended multi-task run.

Any failure of either call is treated as the read not taken: the runner carries on with the task from `requirements.md`, the context file, and the live material, printing no fixed line. The inline `complete-task` skill tells the user in prose that the past-work read failed, quoting the one `Error:` line verbatim, as `ask-in-milestone-context` does; the `complete-task` agent, whose only final messages are `DONE` and `FAILED:`, carries on and reports nothing about it. Keeps the read what the goal calls it, discretionary, so its failure costs no more than not taking it and never stops a task or an unattended run, with no new fixed line, table row, or test, and follows the one existing precedent for a discretionary read of past work. In the agent, the dominant completion path, the failure leaves no trace in any message or file, so a task can be completed against a criterion the read would have fixed with nobody told, and a field measurement of whether the read is taken cannot tell a failed read from one never attempted.

Any failure of either call is treated as the read not taken in both runners alike: the procedure carries on with the task, printing no fixed line and telling nothing in prose, the inline skill included; the only record is the failed call in the run's own transcript. One behaviour for both runners with the least runtime prose — no stop, no line, no inline-only clause — so the inline and isolated runs of the same procedure stay indistinguishable apart from their framing. Even the inline user, who could act on it at no cost, is not told that the read they might rely on failed, and the procedure departs from the plugin's habit of telling a failed call either by a fixed line or in prose.

alternative.id: Fall back to a git read

open-question.alternative: On a failure of either call the runner carries on but substitutes a history read of its own composing on the file (such as `git log` or `git log -p` on the path, or `git show` on the task commit for a `-` line), and only if that too fails carries on without the read; no fixed line is printed and no stop is taken. The runner still gets the why-is-it-this-way evidence the read exists to supply in most failure cases, including the `-` line, whose commit `git show` reads directly. Writes into the procedure the hand-composed git read the milestones tool exists to replace, and confounds the field measurement the goal plans, which must tell the named command run as shown from a history read the agent composed itself; a git-level failure defeats the fallback anyway.

The response depends on where the read is taken: a failure at step 2, on the files the task names up front, stops the task before any edit on a new fixed line with the `Error:` line beneath it (`FAILED:` from the agent); a failure at step 3, on a file met only while editing, is carried on from as the read not taken, told in prose inline and silently in the agent. Stops only where stopping is free and the read can matter most — at step 2 nothing has been edited and the read may fix a criterion of the bar — while never abandoning a half-edited task at step 3, where the bar is already fixed and the read can no longer change it. Two rules for one call, with a new fixed line and table row besides, and the same broken environment that stops one task at step 2 is silently carried past in the next task whose file surfaces only at step 3.

The response depends on which call failed: a failed `tasks <path> --with-body` call stops the task on a new fixed line with its `Error:` line beneath it (`FAILED:` from the agent), since then no past work was read at all; a failed `show <milestone path>` follow-up, the `-` line included, is carried on from with the task lines and bars `tasks` already printed, told in prose inline and silently in the agent. Stops only when the failure points at a broken environment or a wrong path and nothing was learned, while the predictable `show` refusal on a `-` line, and any `show` failure after the bars are already in hand, costs nothing. Two rules split by call where the plugin's other reads treat any failed milestones-tool call as one condition, plus a new fixed line and table row; a decision's own words, which only `show` gives, can be lost without anyone told in the agent.

The procedure names the read and its two commands and says nothing about their failure, leaving it to the procedure's existing opening rule that a failed step is diagnosed, fixed, and retried and never skipped, and beyond that to the runner's judgment, with no fixed line, no prose-telling clause, and no table row. Adds nothing to the procedure, the docs, or the fixed-lines table, and lets the runner fix a mistyped path or step around a `-` line by the rule it already follows for every other failure. Leaves the outcome undetermined across runs and hosts: the opening rule's "never skip a step" pushes a runner toward retrying or returning `FAILED:` on an unfixable read, while another runner will quietly carry on, so neither a harness nor the field measurement can rely on what a failed read leads to.

open-question.question: When the completion procedure's read of past work surfaces an earlier milestone's decision or verified bar that carrying out the task as briefed would undo, and the current milestone's `requirements.md` does not address it, what governs the work: the brief as written, the earlier decision wherever the brief can still be met, or does the runner stop without completing the task?
open-question.alternative: The procedure says the brief as written governs. An earlier milestone's decision or verified bar that the read surfaces is context for how the work is done, and it may fix a criterion only where the brief leaves the point open. Where carrying out the brief undoes it, the brief is carried out and the earlier decision is overridden. The runner does not stop and flags nothing. The bar and the report keep the forms they have now. It extends the ordering the workflow already uses for conflicts to milestones. The current milestone's brief is the later-recorded decision, as `derive-tasks` lets the later `## Decisions` entry govern. It keeps the existing rule against pausing to widen scope, never halts an unattended `complete-all-tasks` run, and leaves the read purely informative, so the procedure gains no branch, no fixed line, and no new stop. The brief may never have been written with the earlier decision in view. `requirements.md` does not address it, and its author may not have known it existed. So an override that nobody chose lands silently in an ordinary `Task-completion:` commit. The only trace is the diff, because the agent returns a bare `DONE` and the body holds only the bar, and the reason for taking the read in the first place, not undoing past work by accident, is lost.

The procedure says the earlier decision governs how the work is done wherever the brief can still be met: among the ways of meeting the brief, the runner picks one that leaves the earlier decision or bar intact, and the read may fix a criterion to that effect. Only where every way of meeting the brief undoes the earlier decision does the brief govern and override it. The runner never stops, and nothing is flagged. It protects past work in every case where protecting it costs the task nothing, which is the case the read most plausibly catches: an incidental shape the brief never meant to change. It also keeps the task completing and the run unattended, with no new stop line and no remedy for an operator to follow. Whether the brief "can still be met" while keeping the earlier decision is a judgment the runner makes alone, and the bar does not have to show it. A runner that leans toward keeping the earlier decision may meet the brief's letter and miss its intent. Where no fit exists, the override still lands silently, just as it does when the brief governs.

The procedure says the earlier decision governs wherever the brief can still be met, exactly as in the fit-else-brief rule. Where every way of meeting the brief would undo it, the runner stops without completing the task. Surfaced at step 2, the stop comes before any edit. Surfaced at step 3, it leaves the tree resumable. The inline `complete-task` reports a new fixed line with the earlier milestone's path or the task commit's hash beneath it. The agent returns `FAILED: <reason>`, which ends a `complete-all-tasks` run on its existing `Task run stopped — a task failed.` line. The remedy is a decision recorded in this milestone's `requirements.md` and then a re-run. A real collision with past work is never settled by a runner alone, in either direction. It goes back to the decision layer, where the workflow puts every choice that is not mechanical. And the many cases that can be accommodated still complete without anyone stepping in. It adds a stop condition, and with it a new row in the fixed-lines table and its test, to a procedure whose only stop so far is the task lookup. It halts an unattended run on a judgment the runner makes itself. The remedy also has no fixed path: the milestone has already passed its no-open-question precondition, so the operator has to bring a question in through a review pass, answer it, and possibly revise the brief, all before the task can complete.

The procedure says any surfaced earlier decision or verified bar that the task as briefed would undo, and that `requirements.md` does not address, stops the runner without completing the task. The runner tries no accommodation, even where the brief could be met another way. The stop takes the same form as in the fit-else-stop rule: before any edit when surfaced at step 2, a resumable tree when surfaced at step 3, a new fixed line for the inline skill, `FAILED: <reason>` from the agent, and a decision recorded in `requirements.md` as the remedy. It is the simplest rule to state and to check afterwards, because the runner judges only whether a collision exists, never whether a compatible way of meeting the brief exists. No past decision is ever overridden, or worked around in a way that strains the brief, without a recorded decision. It stops on collisions the runner could have resolved harmlessly, so an unattended `complete-all-tasks` run halts more often. Each halt costs the operator a review-and-answer cycle on a milestone that had already converged. It also carries the same new fixed line and test that the fit-else-stop rule needs.

The procedure states no rule for this case. A collision the read surfaces is settled under the procedure's existing text: decisions in `requirements.md` bind, and genuine ambiguity is resolved the way the description, the derived bar, and `requirements.md` most plausibly intend. This milestone adds nothing beyond naming the read. It keeps the change to the procedure as small as the goal states, and it adds nothing a later edit would have to keep consistent. It also leaves the field measurement this milestone plans to observe how runners actually handle a collision before any rule is fixed. The existing text never mentions decisions outside `requirements.md`, so each runner chooses between overriding, accommodating, and stopping on its own, and two runs may settle the same collision differently. Since nothing marks which way a run went, a silent override can no more be found afterwards than under the brief-governs rule.

open-question.question: When the completion procedure's step-2 read of past work fixes a criterion of the acceptance bar, does that criterion name what it was formed against (the task commit's hash or the earlier milestone's path), so the read shows in the `Task-completion:` commit body, or is it worded like any other criterion with no reference to the read?
open-question.alternative: A criterion the step-2 read fixes is worded like every other criterion of the bar, as an observable property of the deliverable with no hash, milestone path, or other mention of the read, the same way a criterion a prior task's live deliverable fixes is worded today. Step 2 gains no wording rule for it and step 5's form sentence stays exactly as it is. The bar stays what the task-altitude invariant calls it, a list of checkable properties and nothing beyond them, with no provenance in the text a later reader judges by. The procedure gets no new rule and no runner changes, and no criterion carries a reference that a rebase or amend could leave pointing at nothing. The read leaves no trace in the `Task-completion:` commit, so nothing in history shows a criterion came from past work or which earlier decision it keeps in force. Whether the read was taken can then be seen only in a run's transcript, which matters if the sibling measurement questions count outcomes from commits rather than from transcripts.

Every criterion the step-2 read fixes is required to name what it was formed against, inside its own `- ` bullet: the abbreviated hash from the `tasks` line when a task commit's diff or bar fixed it, and the milestone path from that line's third field when a decision that `show` printed fixed it. Step 2 states the rule once, and step 5's form sentence lets a bullet carry it, so the body is still the bar alone, one bullet per criterion. Each such criterion points at its evidence directly: one `git show <hash>` or one `show <path>` takes a reader to exactly what fixed it, using the identifier the read itself used. The read shows in every `Task-completion:` body that `tasks --with-body` prints back, so the history records it without a transcript. Provenance goes into the bar text, which the project keeps out of recorded `## Decisions` prose on purpose, and a criterion becomes partly a citation rather than purely an observable property. An abbreviated hash stops resolving if a branch is rebased or amended before it merges, and the procedure has to state two reference forms and when each applies.

Every criterion the step-2 read fixes is required to name, inside its own bullet, the milestone path from the third field of the `tasks` line the read went through, whether a task commit's bar or a decision `show` printed fixed it. No hash is ever named. A path is readable and survives rebase and amend, and `show` takes it exactly as written, so the reference stays meaningful as long as history does. One form serves both cases, and the rule takes a single sentence. It is coarser than the evidence: it names the milestone, not the task commit whose bar or diff actually fixed the criterion, so a reader has to search that milestone's tasks again. A task commit that joins no single milestone prints `-` in that field and leaves nothing to name, and a finished milestone's slug can be defined again at the same path later, so `show` on the path may then print a different milestone.

Every criterion the step-2 read fixes is required to name, inside its own bullet, the abbreviated hash of the task commit from the `tasks` line it was formed against. That includes a criterion a `show` follow-up fixed, which names the hash of the task commit that led the read to that milestone. No milestone path is named. One uniform reference that always exists, since every read starts from a `tasks` line that prints a hash, including a commit whose milestone field is `-`. It is the most exact pointer: `git show` on it reaches the brief, the bar, and the diff, and from its milestone field the decision. A hash is opaque to someone reading the bar and does not name the decision when a decision rather than a task fixed the criterion, so that link takes a second hop. An abbreviated hash stops resolving after a rebase or amend of the branch, and it can become ambiguous as history grows.

A criterion the step-2 read fixes may name its source inside its own bullet, a hash for a task commit or a milestone path for a decision, when the runner judges that the reference helps a later reader. Otherwise it is worded like any other criterion. The procedure allows the reference and requires it nowhere. The runner can record provenance exactly where it explains a criterion that would otherwise look arbitrary, and keep the bar clean where the criterion speaks for itself, without a rule that fires on every read. Nothing can check it and nothing can rely on it. A body without a reference does not show that no read was taken, so the history cannot be used to count reads, and bodies differ from run to run in a way no reader or test can predict.

The criteria the step-2 read fixes are worded like every other criterion. The body instead ends with one trailing paragraph of `Token: value` lines, one per source the read used, holding the abbreviated hash for a task commit or the milestone path for a decision. The body contract and step 5's form sentence widen to allow this paragraph after the bullets, and both completion runners' body handling carries it. The bar text stays free of provenance, and `tasks --with-body`, `summary`, and `record` print it exactly as now, because every body the milestones tool prints already drops a trailing paragraph of `Token: value` lines. `git log` and `git show` still show which past work fed the bar. It breaks the invariant that the commit body is the bar and nothing else, and it requires edits to the step-5 form sentence and to both runners' calls. A trailer names sources for the bar as a whole, not for a particular criterion. And because the milestones tool drops it, no query through the tool shows the read: counting reads from it means a hand-written `git log`, the hand-rolled read the tool exists to replace.

open-question.question: The completion procedure's read of past work is triggered by a file the task edits rather than creates whose shape the milestone's `requirements.md` does not explain. Does the same trigger cover a file the task deletes, renames, or moves?
open-question.alternative: The trigger stays a change to the content of a file that already exists. `complete-procedure.md` says outright that deleting, renaming, or moving a file takes no read of past work, so the read is never taken for any of the three. A rename or move that also changes the file's content still triggers on that content edit, as any edit does. The trigger is the narrowest one and mechanically plain, so a runner never has to judge whether a removal counts. The sibling question on which runs the field measurement counts gets a clean population: runs that changed the content of a file that already existed. It also keeps the procedure's added text as small as the goal's one-sentence trigger. The most destructive change a task can make goes unchecked. Deleting or relocating a file that an earlier milestone deliberately placed (this repository has one: the host fixture's `milestones.fixture/` container is named so the discovery pattern skips it, and a `CLAUDE.md` invariant explains why) skips exactly the read meant to show why a file is the way it is. The brief and `requirements.md` are then the only guard.

The procedure treats deleting, renaming, or moving a file that already exists as editing it. The read is taken under the same condition as an edit: `requirements.md` does not explain the file's existence or place. It is taken at step 2 for files the task names up front and at step 3 for the rest. The query is `tasks` on the path the file has before the task. The milestones tool's log reads set `log.follow=false`, so the new path carries no history from before the move, while the old path, still in the tree when the read is taken, lists every task commit that changed it. Every change that undoes something already standing gets the same check before it is made. That includes removals, where an earlier decision that put the file there is most easily lost without anyone noticing. The tool needs no change: the old path exists in the tree when the read is taken, and `tasks` exits 0 on it whatever it lists. The trigger gets wider and the procedure's prose longer. It needs a clause naming which path to read, because reading the new path silently returns only the move commit. More completion runs then take a read whose output can be large: the sibling question on bounding large reads covers this. The measurement population sibling must decide whether these runs count.

The procedure treats deleting a file that already exists as editing it, under the same condition that `requirements.md` does not explain the file's existence. The read is `tasks` on that path, taken before the deletion. A pure rename or move, with the content unchanged, takes no read. The procedure says so, because the file's shape survives under its new path. The read targets the one case where the file's shape is lost outright and an earlier decision behind it cannot be seen in the tree afterwards. Renames and moves get no read, and no clause is needed about which path to read, since a deleted file has only the one path. Location can be a decision too: a name or place chosen so that a pattern matches or skips it, or a path other files cite. Such a decision is broken by a rename or move without a read. The line drawn between deletion and relocation is also one more distinction the runner has to apply and the measurement has to tell apart.

The procedure keeps the trigger worded as the goal states it, "a file the task edits rather than creates", and says nothing about deletions, renames, or moves. Whether one of these counts as an edit is left to the runner's reading on each run. The discretionary read is taken or not as that reading falls. No wording is added and no position is fixed before the field measurement has shown how runners actually treat these cases. The read is discretionary anyway, so the measurement can show whether a stated rule is needed. Runners will read "edits" differently, so the same deletion triggers the read in one run and not in another. For renames, a runner that does take the read may query the new path and get nothing, because the tool follows no rename. The measurement's counted population, owned by a sibling question, also becomes ambiguous for exactly these runs.

open-question.question: The completion procedure's read of past work is triggered by a file whose shape the milestone's `requirements.md` does not explain. Does a shape the project's context file explains (in this repository, a `CLAUDE.md` invariant) count as explained, so that no read is taken, or does only `requirements.md` count?
open-question.alternative: Only the milestone's `requirements.md` counts as explaining a file's shape: its goal, its `## Relevant starting state`, and its recorded decisions. What the context file says about the file, however fully it gives the reason (in this repository a `CLAUDE.md` invariant), does not count, so an edited file whose shape `requirements.md` does not explain triggers the `tasks <path> --with-body` read even when the context file explains it. The procedure says this in one clause of its trigger sentence. It matches the goal's wording exactly and gives a trigger a runner can check against one document already read whole at step 2. The read still fires on core files that a project's context file documents heavily, which is where an earlier milestone's decision most likely sits and where the context file's account can lag behind the task commits' bars. This keeps the measured population large enough to decide whether the read stays discretionary. In a project whose context file already gives the reason for a shape, the read repeats what the runner holds. It is paid at the measured sizes (200 lines, 59 KB for `docs/skill-reference.md`, 104 lines for `CLAUDE.md` itself), and in this repository it would fire on nearly every edit of a file under `core/` or `docs/`, since a milestone's `requirements.md` rarely explains files outside its own goal.

Both `requirements.md` and the workspace-root context file count, but the context file counts only where it states why the shape is as it is, for the part of the file the edit changes (for example an invariant giving the reason and saying what must not be restored). A context-file passage that only describes the file, such as a repository-layout entry naming what the file holds, does not count. A shape neither document gives a reason for triggers the read. The procedure says this in its trigger sentence, which then names the context file beside `requirements.md`. It skips the read exactly where the runner already holds the reason for the shape at no extra cost, since step 2 reads the context file whole. It also uses the protection the design draft relies on, finish writing lasting changes into the context file, rather than repeating it with a history read. A description-only mention still leaves the read in force. It goes beyond the goal's literal trigger, which names `requirements.md` alone. It also asks the runner to judge whether a context-file passage gives the reason for the specific element it is changing, which is softer than checking one document. In this repository, whose `CLAUDE.md` gives the reason for most core files, the read would rarely fire, which shrinks the runs the field measurement can count if its population is defined by the trigger.

Both `requirements.md` and the context file count, and the context file counts wherever it gives any account of the file's shape, a description included (a layout entry, a conventions paragraph), not only a stated reason. Only a file that neither document mentions in a way that accounts for its shape triggers the read. It is the easiest form to check. A runner only asks whether the file is accounted for in either document it read at step 2, so the read is reserved for files the project's own documentation leaves uncovered, and its cost on heavily documented files drops to nothing. A description says what a file is, not why an element of it was chosen, so the read is skipped on exactly the documented core files where an earlier milestone's deliberate choice is most likely to be undone. That brings back the risk the read exists to guard against. In this repository almost every tracked file has a `CLAUDE.md` layout entry, so the read would almost never fire.

Any project document the runner reads counts as explaining the shape: `requirements.md`, the context file, `README.md`, the project's docs (in this repository `docs/workflow.md`, `docs/design-claims.md`, and `docs/skill-reference.md`), and a comment in the edited file itself, each counting where it states why the shape is as it is. Only a shape none of them gives a reason for triggers the read. It skips the history read wherever the project's own documentation already holds the reason. That treats the record as a fallback for undocumented shapes only, which keeps the read's cost lowest without counting a bare description as a reason. The set of documents it covers is open-ended, so a runner cannot tell when it has looked far enough to skip the read, and two runners can disagree on the same file. That makes the trigger untestable in the sense the design draft asked for ("the trigger is testable without the record"). It also departs furthest from the goal's wording, and it still lets a document's account, which may be out of date, stand in for the task commits' bars.

The explanation condition is dropped: every file the task edits rather than creates triggers the `tasks <path> --with-body` read, whatever `requirements.md` or the context file says about it. No document counts as explaining, and the runner judges nothing before reading. The trigger becomes fully mechanical. A transcript shows whether it was met from the edits alone, so the field measurement needs no reader to judge which runs met it, and no past decision is missed because a document's account of the file was incomplete or stale. It contradicts the goal's recorded trigger and would need a goal revision. It also pays the full read on every edit of an existing file, prints of tens of kilobytes on the most-changed files that grow with every task, unless a bound is placed on large reads, an axis the sibling question on large reads owns.

The procedure takes no position on the context file. The trigger sentence keeps the goal's wording, a shape `requirements.md` does not explain, with no clause saying whether the context file or any other document counts, so each runner decides for itself whether something it read elsewhere explains the shape. It adds no prose and no rule to the procedure. Runners use their judgment of what they already hold, and the field measurement can show how they actually read the trigger before the wording is fixed. Runners will read the trigger differently. The measurement cannot tell a read skipped because the runner judged the context file sufficient from a read skipped for no reason, and whether that matters depends on how the measured run population is defined, an axis a sibling question owns. The question stays open in the runtime prose rather than being settled.

open-question.question: With the milestones tool unchanged, does the completion procedure bound its `tasks <path> --with-body` read on a file that many task commits changed, or is the read taken whole whatever it prints? Measured on 2026-11-10 it prints 200 lines (59,079 bytes) for `docs/skill-reference.md` and 104 lines (31,521 bytes) for `CLAUDE.md`, and it grows with every later task that changes the file.
open-question.alternative: The procedure shows the full fixed `tasks <path> --with-body` command with no pipe, flag, or size rule, and the runner takes its whole print whatever its length. No bound is added in this milestone. If the print's size later proves a problem, a later milestone revisits it, most directly by giving the tool a bound of its own as `milestones` has `--last N`. Matches the goal as written, with one fixed command and no shell code beside it, and the runner sees every past task and bar that touched the file, so no relevant decision is cut off. The read is discretionary and taken only for an edited file whose shape `requirements.md` does not explain, so the large prints come only when the runner chooses to read, and they are bounded by the project's own history (59 KB at most for any file in this repository today). For the files most often edited, the print is already 30 to 60 KB (`docs/skill-reference.md` 59,079 bytes, `CLAUDE.md` 31,521 bytes) and grows with every task that changes them. In the isolated `complete-task` agent it is paid once per task that triggers the read, on top of the context file and `requirements.md` read whole, and the oldest entries, the ones least likely to bear, take up as much room as the newest.

The procedure's fixed command pipes the whole `tasks <path> --with-body` print through `head -n N` with a literal N stated once in the procedure (on the order of 100 lines). The runner reads only the newest lines up to that count, since the query prints newest first. The tool is unchanged, and the cut ignores where one commit's bar ends and the next begins. The simplest bound to state and to follow: one short pipe on the shown command, the same on every host. It caps the read's cost at a known size however large the file's history grows, and it keeps the newest past work, which is the most likely to explain the file's present shape. The cut can fall in the middle of a bar, leaving a criterion partly shown, and nothing in the print says older entries were dropped. When `head` closes the pipe early the tool can die on a broken pipe and write a traceback to stderr, while the pipeline's exit status is `head`'s. That blurs what counts as a failed read, which the failure-handling sibling question owns. The pipe also changes the fixed command shape the literal-command and measurement siblings count against.

The procedure's fixed command pipes the `tasks <path> --with-body` print through a short fixed filter (an `awk` program counting column-0 lines) that keeps the N newest task commits, each with its whole bar, and drops the rest. N is a literal stated in the procedure, on the order of the review pass's `--last 10`. The filter relies on the query's own boundary rule, under which every column-0 line starts a new task and every bar line is indented. The tool is unchanged. Bounds the read by the unit the reader reasons in, a past task, so no bar is ever cut partway and every kept entry is complete. It needs no tool change: the column-0 boundary was designed so one simple parser reads `--with-body`, and the procedure can state that boundary in one line. Adds a small hand-written program to a runtime command, the kind of shell code the tools exist to replace, though it is shown fixed rather than re-typed each run. It is the most intricate command any runtime file passes to the milestones tool, and it carries the same broken-pipe exposure as any early-closing filter if written to stop reading. Ten commits with bars can still exceed 30 KB on the busiest files, so the cap is set in commits, not in bytes.

The procedure's first read is `tasks <path>` without `--with-body`, taken whole: one line per task commit with its hash, date, milestone path, and title. The runner then reads bars only for the commits whose titles bear on the edit, each by its hash through `git show -s --format=%b <hash>` (or `git show <hash>` when the diff's removed brief is wanted), with `show <milestone path>` kept as the follow-up for a decision's own words. Whether `--with-body` is still taken whole when the title list is short is stated once in the procedure. The tool is unchanged. Bounds the read by relevance rather than by recency or a count. The title list is small (one short line per commit, 39 lines for `docs/skill-reference.md`), so an old but bearing bar is still reachable, and an irrelevant one is never loaded. It mirrors the two-tier pattern the starting-state procedure and the review pass already use: an overview line first, then a deeper read only where a line bears. Moves away from the goal, which names `tasks <path> --with-body` as the read. The bar step becomes a git command the procedure composes outside the milestones tool, which is exactly the kind of read the measurement siblings count as a hand-composed history read, and its per-commit body read gets none of the tool's trailer stripping. Each bearing commit costs another call, and judging relevance from a title alone can miss a bar whose title gives no hint.

open-question.question: Does the completion procedure's `tasks <path> --with-body` read carry the clause the review pass and the starting-state procedure put on their milestones-tool calls — the command written out in full, never through a variable, alias, or function of the runner's own — or does it show the full command with no such clause, as the other nine runtime files calling the milestones tool do?
open-question.alternative: `core/shared/complete-procedure.md` shows the full fixed command `python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/milestones.py tasks <path> --with-body` and puts the starting-state procedure's clause on it once, in the sentence that introduces the read: every milestones-tool call the read makes, the `tasks` call on each file it is taken for and the `show <milestone path>` follow-up alike, is written out in full on every call, never through a variable, alias, or function of the runner's own defined to stand for the command or any part of it. The `CLAUDE.md` shell-literal invariant gains the completion procedure among the sites carrying the clause, and the rebuilt host trees carry the sentence. The read qualifies under the invariant's own scoping rule, since a runner that takes it may call the tool several times in one task (one `tasks` per edited file, then `show`), and it runs in the population most given to rewriting commands, the completion agents of whom about three in four wrote an ad-hoc script in the 202 measured runs; a tool command held in a variable runs as one word naming no command under zsh, so the clause guards exactly the shortening this runner is likeliest to make, and it puts the procedure on the same footing as the other two discretionary multi-call readers of the milestones tool. It adds a sentence and an invariant entry for a failure no completion run has yet shown on this read, and it makes the clause no longer a marker of the two runners that call the tool on every pass; a measured run that wraps the command in a variable then reads as breaking a stated rule rather than as evidence of whether the clause was needed, which bears on what the field measurement's outcomes tell apart (owned by the sibling questions on measured outcomes).

`core/shared/complete-procedure.md` shows the full fixed command `python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/milestones.py tasks <path> --with-body`, and names `show <milestone path>` as its follow-up, with no sentence about writing the command out in full or never through a variable, alias, or function, as the nine other runtime files calling the milestones tool show theirs. The `CLAUDE.md` shell-literal invariant's list of clause sites stays unchanged. It keeps the procedure's addition to the read itself and leaves the shell-literal invariant untouched, the rule staying scoped to the sites where the failure was seen or where the tool is called on every pass; the discretionary read is called at most a few times per task on one quoted path, so no path list can be split, and the field measurement then observes unprompted whether completion runners shorten this command, which is the evidence a later clause would rest on. The read is a multi-call use of a tool command by the runners most prone to rewriting commands, the case the invariant's rationale names, so a runner that holds the command in a variable gets a call naming no command under zsh, and a discretionary read that fails that way may simply be dropped or replaced by a hand-composed `git log`, a deviation the measurement would then count against the read itself; how such a failure is handled is owned by the sibling question on a failed past-work read.

open-question.question: In the field measurement that decides whether the completion procedure's read of past work stays discretionary, which completion runs is the read counted against: every completion run, only runs that edited a file that already existed, or only runs a reader judges to have met the trigger (an edited file whose shape `requirements.md` does not explain), which no transcript shows mechanically?
open-question.alternative: The read is counted against every completion run in the measured run set, whatever the task touched. No trigger filter is applied: a run that only created files counts the same as one that edited files with a long history. Fully mechanical and impossible to argue with. Every `Task-completion:` commit and every completion transcript is in the population, so the denominator needs no diff parse and no judgment, and anyone re-running the scripts gets the same count. The trigger is a file the task edits rather than creates whose shape `requirements.md` does not explain, so every run that never met it counts as one where the read was not taken. That dilutes the rate with correct non-reads. Under a rule keyed on any miss or a share of runs, the read could be made required just because many tasks only create files, which the discretionary design meant to allow.

The read is counted only against runs that modified a file that already existed. This is read mechanically from each run's `Task-completion:` commit as a path with modify status (`git diff --diff-filter=M` on the commit, or the equivalent from the transcript's edit calls). The milestone's own `TASKS_TODO.md`, which every completion commit modifies, and the milestone's other files are left out. Whether `requirements.md` explains the file's shape is not judged. It follows the half of the trigger that can be checked by machine, edited rather than created, so runs that only created files no longer count as misses. It stays reproducible from the commits alone, with no reader in the loop and no transcript interpretation. It still counts runs whose edited file `requirements.md` does explain, where skipping the read is the correct behaviour, so it overstates misses. How much depends on how often tasks edit files the milestone's own decisions already describe. Whether a deleted, renamed, or moved file joins the population depends on how the trigger for removed files is settled, and that is a sibling question.

The read is counted only against runs that modified an existing file (milestone files excluded, as above) whose path `requirements.md` does not mention, as that file stood at the run's start. The mention test is a mechanical text search of the requirements file at the commit's parent. It stands in for "does not explain", and no reader judges the shape. It tracks both halves of the trigger while staying a script: a file the milestone's decisions name is presumed explained. So it removes the most obvious correct non-reads without any reader judgment, and the count can be re-run later. Being mentioned is not the same as being explained. A decision can name a file without accounting for its shape, and a shape can be explained without its path ever appearing (by module name, by a directory, or in the context file), so the proxy misclassifies in both directions in ways nobody has measured. Whether a context-file explanation should count is a sibling question's axis that the proxy ignores either way.

The read is counted only against runs that a reader judges to have met the trigger. Among the runs that modified an existing file (milestone files excluded), the reader reads `requirements.md` as it stood at the run's start and decides, per edited file, whether it explains that file's shape. Only runs with at least one unexplained edited file are counted. It measures exactly what the procedure asks of the runner, so a miss means a run that should have read past work and did not. That is the cleanest evidence for or against making the read required. No transcript shows the trigger mechanically, so the population rests on judgment for every edited-file run. That costs reading time on every such run, invites the measurer's bias about the outcome into the denominator, and may not be reproducible when the figures are checked again later. What counts as explained also depends on how the context-file trigger question is settled.

The population starts as the mechanical set of runs that modified an existing file (milestone files excluded). Every such run that took a history read counts as is. Only the runs that took no read are judged against `requirements.md` as it stood at the run's start, and a run whose edited files it explained is dropped from the population. Judgment is spent only where it changes the verdict, on the runs that would otherwise count as misses. That is a small share of the reader's effort compared with judging every run, and it still keeps correct non-reads from being counted as failures. The two sides are tested differently. A run that read past work without needing to is kept, while an equivalent run that skipped it is dropped, so the read rate is biased upward. The judged half carries the same reproducibility and bias risk as fully reader-judged counting.

The read is counted against more than one population at once: every completion run, and the mechanical subset that modified an existing file (milestone files excluded). Optionally a third, the reader-judged trigger subset, is added over the same runs. Each count is reported side by side in the measurement's result. It shows how much the trigger narrows the population and how the rate changes from one population to the next, so a later reader can tell a real miss rate from dilution. The mechanical populations stay reproducible even if the judged one is not. It does not settle which population the decision is made on. That rule has to name one, and naming it is part of the result-requiring-the-read question, a sibling. Without it, the side-by-side figures leave room to pick whichever population supports the preferred outcome. Each extra population also adds counting work.

open-question.question: In the field measurement that decides whether the completion procedure's read of past work stays discretionary, which outcomes are told apart for each counted run — for instance the named `tasks` command run as shown, a history read the agent composed itself (`git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` on the file), and no history read at all?
open-question.alternative: Each counted run gets exactly one of two outcomes: the procedure's full fixed `python3 …/tools/milestones.py tasks <path> --with-body` command run on a file the task edits, matched by its command string in the run's tool-call records, or not. Everything else, a milestones-tool call in another form, a history read the agent composed with `git log`, `git blame`, or `git show`, and no history read at all, falls into the one "not run as shown" outcome; the `show` follow-up, a failed call, and a run doing several reads are not told apart. The cheapest and most mechanical classification there is: one string match per run over the tool-call records `host.records` already reads into one shape on all three hosts, with no reader judgment, and it matches the draft's rule exactly where both "never made" and "made by hand" lead to the same result. It cannot tell an agent that hand-rolled a `git log -p` from one that read no history at all, nor a tool call in a slightly wrong form from no read, so the measurement shows that the read failed but not which way, and any result rule that treats the two failures differently has nothing to count; viable only where the rule set under "Result requiring the read" needs no more than made-as-shown against not.

Each counted run gets one of three outcomes: tool read (any milestones-tool `tasks` call on an edited file's path, whatever its spelling, flags, or exit status), hand-composed read (a `git log`, `git blame`, `git show`, or `git diff` the agent wrote naming the edited file's path, a `git show` of a hash the tool's own print supplied counting as the tool read's follow-up and not as hand-composed), or no history read. A run holding both a tool read and a hand-composed read counts as a tool read. It tells apart exactly the three outcomes the draft names ("never made or made by hand"), stays mechanical over the tool-call records, and does not penalize an agent that ran the tool and then followed a printed hash into its diff, the one-`git show` follow-up the `tasks` output is designed to support. A run that took the tool read and also composed its own `git log -p` on the same file reads as a success, so hand-rolling beside the tool, the pattern the tool exists to end, stays invisible, and a `tasks` call without `--with-body` or written through a variable counts the same as the command as shown.

The same three outcomes as above, tool read, hand-composed read, and no history read, with the same rule that a `git show` of a hash the tool printed is the tool read's follow-up, but a run holding any hand-composed read of an edited file's history counts as hand-composed even when it also ran the `tasks` command. It is the strict reading of the draft's failure mode: any composed `git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` on the file is the ad-hoc pattern the tools exist to end, so no run that hand-rolled is counted as a success, while the outcome set stays three classes a script assigns mechanically. An agent that ran the tool and then legitimately widened the read by hand, say `git blame` on a line the task commits did not explain, counts as a failure, which can push the result toward making the read required for behaviour that was the tool read working as intended; the hash-follow-up exemption also needs the script to match hashes against the tool's printed output, which a plain command match does not do.

Each counted run gets one of four outcomes: tool read only, hand-composed read only, both a tool read and a hand-composed read, or no history read, the classes defined as in the three-outcome options (any `tasks` call on an edited file's path is a tool read; a composed `git log`, `git blame`, `git show`, or `git diff` naming the file is hand-composed; a `git show` of a hash the tool printed is the tool read's follow-up), with no precedence rule needed. It keeps the co-occurrence visible instead of resolving it by a precedence the plan has to defend, so the result can tell "agents skip the tool", "agents replace it", and "agents supplement it" apart while each run still gets one mechanically assigned outcome. The "both" class mixes legitimate widening with hand-rolling beside the tool, so a large "both" share still needs a reader to interpret, and like the three-outcome options it counts a `tasks` call in any form, a missing `--with-body` or a call through a variable included, as the tool read.

Each counted run gets one outcome from an ordered list, the first matching class winning: the `tasks <path> --with-body` command as shown (the full fixed command, written out literally, on an edited file's path), the milestones tool in another form (`tasks` without `--with-body`, `record` or another query on the file, a relative or variable-held tool path, an alias or function standing for the command), a hand-composed `git log`, `git blame`, `git show`, or `git diff` naming the file (a `git show` of a tool-printed hash being the tool read's follow-up), or no history read. A failed call counts under the form it was written in, and the `show <milestone path>` follow-up is recorded beside the outcome as a yes or no, not as an outcome of its own. It is the only single-outcome classification that measures whether the read is taken as shown, which is what the goal's "full fixed command shown" and the literal-command rule are for, so drift into a near-miss form (the most likely failure for a discretionary step written vaguely) shows as its own count rather than passing as success. The "another form" class needs a hand-maintained list of near-miss spellings that a script has to match, and its value depends on what the procedure demands of the command's spelling, the axis the "Literal-command clause" question owns; the ordering also hides a hand-composed read in any run that called the tool in some form.

No single outcome per run: every history read in a counted run is classified and attributed to the edited file it reads, and the run is reported as the set of classes it holds. The classes are the `tasks` command as shown, the milestones tool in another form, the `show <milestone path>` follow-up, a `git show` of a hash the tool printed, a hand-composed `git log`, `git blame`, `git show`, or `git diff` on the file (each git command counted separately), and a failed milestones-tool call; a run holding none of them is the no-history-read run, and any summary outcome is derived from the tallies afterwards. It keeps every distinction a later result rule could need, whatever rule the "Result requiring the read" question settles on, and lets the figures be re-cut later without re-reading the transcripts, the property the earlier measurements lost when their scripts and reports left `temp/`. It is the most work to script and to read: per-file attribution means matching each command to an edited path, the counts no longer answer the question in one line, and a result rule still has to state which tally combination counts as "never made" or "made by hand", so the classification decision is moved onto the result rule rather than settled here.

open-question.question: Over which runs is the field measurement of the completion procedure's read of past work taken: which projects and hosts, starting from which plugin release, and how many completion runs at the least before its result is read?

What measured result makes the completion procedure's read of past work a required step instead of a discretionary one: any counted run in which the read was not taken or was composed by hand, a stated share of the counted runs, or another rule?
open-question.alternative: The plan fixes the rule in advance and pools both failure kinds: the read becomes a required step if any single counted run either took no history read or composed its own (a `git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` in place of the named `tasks` command). The threshold is one run. It is the simplest rule to apply, since one run settles it and no share, count, or judgment needs stating. It also matches the draft's sentence "the call never made or made by hand" read run by run, and it treats a hand-rolled read with the same zero tolerance that led to the task-list and fold tools. One outlier run decides the whole question, so the measurement can hardly come out any other way. That makes it a near-certain route to the required form the draft set aside for costing a call on every task. How often it fires depends on the population the sibling question fixes: counted over every completion run, a missed read would be found almost at once even where the trigger never applied.

The plan fixes the rule in advance and pools both failure kinds: the read becomes required when the counted runs that took no read or composed their own reach a stated share below half. The share is set low enough to fall under the earlier measured failure rates, for instance one counted run in four. It tolerates an occasional slip but still fires at failure rates like the ones earlier tools were built on: about three in four measured completion agents wrote their own move script, and 42% of measured folds were ad-hoc scripts. A discretionary read failing that often would be judged by the same standard as those earlier hand-rolled steps. The exact share is a judgment fixed before any data exists, and the plan has to defend it. A share only means something over enough runs, which ties it to the minimum run count the measurement-run-set question fixes. It is also open to the same population effect as a zero threshold: if runs where no read was needed are counted, the share rises.

The plan fixes the rule in advance and pools both failure kinds: the read becomes required only when more than half of the counted runs took no read or composed their own. The read becomes required, and every task pays the call, only once the evidence plainly shows the discretionary form failing in most runs. That is the strongest case for overturning the draft's own reasoning against the required form. A read missed or hand-rolled in as many as 42% of runs (the fold rate that was enough to justify the fold tool) stays discretionary. So the plan accepts a failure rate the project has already treated as reason to act elsewhere. Like any share, it needs the minimum run count the measurement-run-set question fixes.

The plan fixes the rule in advance: the read becomes required only if no counted run took the named `tasks` command as shown, so that the read is never made as written across the whole measurement. This is the draft's "the call never made" read literally, applied to the whole run set rather than run by run. It is the most decisive result possible. If the named command never appears in any counted run, nothing shows that the discretionary mention works, and the case for making the read required is beyond dispute. It almost never fires. One correct run keeps the read discretionary no matter how many other runs skipped it or hand-rolled it, so the measurement would leave in place exactly the silent failure the draft says a discretionary read invites.

The plan fixes the rule in advance and treats the two failure kinds separately. Any counted run that composed its own history read in place of the named command makes the read required by itself. A run that took no read counts toward a stated share below half, and the read becomes required when that share is reached. Each failure kind gets the tolerance it deserves. A hand-composed `git log` is exactly the ad-hoc pattern the full command was shown to prevent, and it is visible in a transcript without any judgment. A run with no read may be a correct skip on a file with nothing behind it, so it is weighed as a rate and not as a single event. Two rules are harder to state and to apply than one, and the zero-tolerance half carries the outlier risk of a one-run threshold. The rule also assumes the measurement tells the two outcomes apart, which the measured-read-outcomes question settles.

The plan fixes the rule in advance and counts only runs that took no history read: the read becomes required when those runs reach a stated share below half of the counted runs. A run that composed its own `git log`, `git blame`, or `git show` counts as having taken the read, so it does not count toward making the step required. The result is matched to the remedy. Making the step required cures a skipped read but not a misspelled one, since a required step can still be written by hand. So only omission is counted against the discretionary form, and a hand-rolled read, which would need a different fix, is not. It departs from the draft's stated rule, which counts a hand-rolled read as a failure. This plan would also give hand-rolled reads no consequence, so the pattern the milestones tool exists to end could persist unmeasured against any threshold. Like any share, it needs the minimum run count the measurement-run-set question fixes.

The plan states what is counted and over which runs but fixes no threshold. The milestone that reads the measurement decides whether the read becomes required, weighing the reported figures as milestones 46 and 48 weighed theirs, against the cost of a call on every task. No number is committed to before the shape of the data is known. That is how the two earlier field measurements were actually used: figures weighed against an estimated saving, not checked against a threshold stated beforehand. It leaves out what the goal says the plan carries, "the result that makes the read required", so it amounts to rejecting part of the goal. It also leaves the outcome open to a reading shaped by whatever the later milestone prefers, the risk a preset rule exists to remove.

open-question.question: Where are the scripts and the report of the field measurement of the completion procedure's read of past work kept, so that its figures can be checked again later: under the git-ignored `temp/`, where the reports and scripts of the two earlier field measurements stood and no longer do, in a tracked location, or does the plan in `ideas/milestones_addressed_by_path.md` leave it unstated?
open-question.alternative: The plan in `ideas/milestones_addressed_by_path.md` states that the measurement's scripts and its report are kept under the git-ignored `temp/`, as the two earlier field measurements' were, and that only the resulting figures are carried into the `requirements.md` of the milestone that decides on them (and into `CLAUDE.md` if an invariant cites them); nothing of the evidence is committed. Nothing derived from field transcripts of other projects, their paths, task titles, or wording, enters this repository's history, and no new tracked location or layout entry is needed: it follows the precedent exactly and costs nothing to state. It is the arrangement under which both earlier reports and the `answer-sweep-analysis/` scripts are already gone from `temp/`, so the figures could again be checked later only as the numbers a `requirements.md` quotes, never recomputed or audited for what was counted; the stated aim of the question, re-checking the figures, is not met.

The plan states that the scripts and the report are committed in this repository under `ideas/`, next to `ideas/milestones_addressed_by_path.md` (for instance in one subdirectory named for the measurement), so the plan and its evidence stand together; the raw transcripts themselves are not committed. The evidence is versioned and reviewable in the open with no new top-level directory and no new `CLAUDE.md` layout entry, and a later reader of the plan finds the counting scripts and the report one directory away from it. `ideas/` is documented as design drafts that precede any milestone, so a measurement report and its scripts stretch that directory's stated purpose; whatever the report quotes from other projects' runs becomes part of this repository's tracked history, and the scripts can be re-run only while the transcripts they read still exist.

alternative.id: Both in a dedicated tracked directory

open-question.alternative: The plan states that the scripts and the report are committed in this repository under a new tracked directory reserved for field-measurement evidence (one subdirectory per measurement), which the `CLAUDE.md` repository layout gains an entry for; the raw transcripts are not committed. It gives this and every later field measurement one stable, purpose-named home, so the figures the plugin's invariants cite (the 202 completion agents, the 856 answers) have a place to be checked from again instead of each measurement choosing ad hoc. It adds a tracked directory and a layout entry, a standing convention, for what this milestone needs once, and it carries the same exposure of other projects' run details in tracked history; the scripts again depend on transcripts kept nowhere in the repository.

The plan states that the counting scripts are committed in a tracked location of this repository while the report stays under the git-ignored `temp/`, its figures carried into the deciding milestone's `requirements.md` as before. The method, which run is counted and how each outcome is told apart, survives and can be re-run on the same or a later set of transcripts, while the report's project-specific findings stay out of tracked history. The exact report the decision rested on is still lost the way the earlier ones were, so re-checking a quoted figure means re-running the scripts, which works only while the transcripts that produced it are still on disk.

The plan states that the report, including the counting rule written out in prose and the per-run tallies its figures are summed from, is committed in a tracked location of this repository, while the scripts that produced it stay under the git-ignored `temp/` as throwaway code. The figures can be checked later against the tallies the report records, with no dependence on transcripts that may since have aged out, and no one-off analysis code is added to a repository whose tracked Python is otherwise tested tools. Re-deriving the figures from the runs themselves means writing the counting again from the report's prose, so an error in the scripts that shaped the tallies can no longer be found; the tallies also carry other projects' run details into tracked history.

The plan states that the scripts and the report are kept in a versioned location outside this repository, such as the separate benchmark project that `ideas/benchmark_for_cairn.md` describes or a private repository of the maintainer's, and the deciding milestone's `requirements.md` records the figures together with where that evidence lives. The evidence is versioned and can be checked again, while material derived from other projects' transcripts stays out of the plugin's own, possibly public, history. The benchmark project does not exist yet and any other repository is one more thing to keep, so the evidence lives where this repository's record can only point at it and nothing here guarantees it survives; a reader of the plan cannot follow the pointer without access.

The plan in `ideas/milestones_addressed_by_path.md` names what is counted, over which runs, and the result that makes the read required, as the goal lists, and says nothing about where the scripts or the report are kept, leaving that to whoever takes the measurement; the figures still reach the deciding milestone's `requirements.md` as that milestone's decisions. It keeps the plan to exactly the three things the goal requires it to carry and commits this milestone to no storage convention for work that will be done later, possibly on a different machine or under the benchmark project. With nothing stated, the default is what happened before, a scratch directory that is later emptied, so the figures that decide whether the read becomes required are likely to survive only as quoted numbers that cannot be checked again.
